title: On-prem air-gapped deployment deep dive
summary: Redwood SE and AE walked Acme Biotech through the on-prem / air-gapped delivery plan: offline artifact bundle (containers + drivers), offline licensing approach, signed checksums and GPG signatures, GPU driver compatibility matrix, and an installation runbook. Discussed KV cache persistence, batching/latency tradeoffs, quantization profiles and impact on throughput, and benchmarking plan for pilot. Agreed next steps: Redwood to deliver offline bundle and driver matrix, Acme to schedule pilot window and share GPU inventory and security requirements.
topics: air-gapped install process and checksums/GPG signing
quantization profiles and accuracy regression checks
next_steps: Maya Patel | Send offline install bundle (container tarball + signed SHA256 checksums) | 2025-02-18
Carlos Jimenez | Share GPU driver compatibility matrix and recommended CUDA/cuDNN versions | 2025-02-17
Acme Biotech (Lina) | Provide inventory of GPU nodes, OS versions, and air-gap constraints | 2025-02-19

transcript: Header: 2025-02-12 15:00 UTC | Duration: 57 minutes | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Lina, Mark, Priya, Samir (Acme)
[00:00] Maya: Hi everyone uh thanks for joining this deep dive on the on-prem air gap flow, we'll focus on artifact delivery, drivers, and the offline licensing path
[00:15] Lina: Thanks, yeah we're especially concerned about no internet installs, our procurement requires signed binaries and an approval chain, so we need the exact bundle and checksums

[00:30] Carlos: Totally makes sense; our offline bundle is a tar.gz that contains OCI images exported via 'docker save', driver packages (rpm/deb), an install.sh, and a signed manifest SHA256 sums and GPG signature. We can also provide an md5 if your pipeline needs it - though sha256 is preferred
[00:50] Mark: Quick q, do you build your containers with CUDA in them or do you rely on host drivers? Some of our nodes have driver locked to 470, others have 525

[01:05] Carlos: Good question; we rely on host CUDA drivers for kernel modules. Containers are built against ABI targets; we have a compatibility matrix. For older drivers like 470 we have a fallback runtime image compiled with older libcudnn. We'll share that matrix, but host driver compatibility is a hard req for GPU functionality
[01:30] Priya: From security side we need an offline licensing mechanism; no phone-home. How do you manage license activation and revocation offline?

[01:45] Maya: Our offline license flow uses signed license files that embed customer ID and expiry, signed with our private key. You'll verify with our public key included in the bundle. For revocation we can issue a revocation file distributed during maintenance windows — it is not realtime but aligns with enterprise air-gap practices
[02:05] Lina: Is there an option for HSM integration or KMS inside their network for key storage? We can't store private keys in plain files

[02:20] Carlos: We support integrating with customer KMS/HSM for the runtime node — the runtime can be configured with a KMS endpoint or to talk to a proxy that you run internally. For fully air-gapped we also provide instructions to use the hardware HSM on host or an offline keystore with strict ACLs
[02:45] Samir: How do you handle updates? We don't want to be rebuilding images frequently; what's the patch path?

[02:55] Maya: We provide patch bundles and versioned tarballs. For security patches you can choose to pull the patch tar from a staging network segment, apply, validate, and then promote to production; Redwood can produce a delta bundle to reduce size
[03:15] Mark: On the runtime side, we care about KV cache warm-up. If nodes restart in an air-gapped cluster, how fast does KV cache warm up, do you persist cache to disk?

[03:30] Carlos: Currently we persist KV cache snapshots to disk optionally; it's configurable. For example you can enable periodic checkpointing of KV-cache to a local disk path; on startup the runtime restores the KV cache which drastically reduces cold-start token generation latency. There's a tradeoff with disk I/O and state size — we'll share recommended checkpoint frequencies
[03:55] Mark: Nice. Is the persisted cache portable between versions? If we roll model from v1 to v1.1 will the cache still be valid?

[04:10] Carlos: It depends on tokenizer changes and attention formats; minor patches typically work but we treat the checkpoint as a best-effort compatibility. Major architecture changes require cache invalidation. We tag snapshots with model hash and runtime version so the runtime won't load incompatible snapshots
[04:30] Maya: Also for air-gap we can include a small priming dataset so you can pre-populate KV with common prefixes relevant to your workloads before going live
[04:50] Priya: Quantization — we've seen accuracy degradation. Do you provide quantized model artifacts in the bundle or do you expect us to run quantize steps on-prem?

[05:05] Carlos: We can supply quantized variants (4-bit, 8-bit) pre-compiled into the runtime format. For on-prem we recommend starting with our recommended Q4 profile for throughput and only do Q8 or full fp16 if accuracy regressions occur. We'll include eval sets and a small eval harness to run locally and compare outputs
[05:35] Lina: For benchmarking, what metrics should we collect? Latency p95, throughput tokens/s, GPU utilization, and KV cache hit rates?

[05:50] Carlos: Exactly p50/p95 latency, tokens/sec, GPU SM utilization, GPU memory breakdown, batch size distribution, KV cache hit/miss ratio. We'll provide a sample benchmarking script that logs these and uploads results to a CSV you can review offline
[06:10] Mark: About batching — our interactive workload needs 100ms p95. What's the tradeoff if we enable larger micro-batches to increase throughput?

[06:25] Carlos: Batching increases throughput at cost of tail latency. We have continuous small-batch strategies in the runtime that form micro-batches within a latency SLO window; you can set a max latency budget per request. For 100ms p95 you likely want small batch sizes (1-4) and low batching window. For throughput-heavy offline jobs, larger batch sizes are optimal
[06:50] Maya: We'll include a recommended config template for latency-sensitive endpoints vs batch endpoints. You can tune target_latency_ms and max_batch_size
[07:05] Samir: Driver installation — are you providing vendor-specific driver packages? Our nodes use RHEL 8 and 9, no apt available

[07:20] Carlos: Yes we provide rpm packages for NVIDIA drivers and recommended kernel module versions. We also include DKMS instructions if you need to rebuild modules. For very locked down kernels we can provide pre-built kernel modules but that requires eval access to your kernel ABI — we'll need the exact uname and kernel-devel versions
[07:45] Priya: We require signed packages and reproducible checksums. How are signatures provided?

[07:55] Carlos: All tarballs and packages will be signed with our GPG key. We'll include the public key and instructions for verification using gpg --verify and sha256sum -c. We'll also provide an SHA256 signed manifest file
[08:15] Mark: For GPU driver compatibility matrix, will you assert required driver minimums for certain quantization paths?

[08:30] Carlos: Yes; some quantization kernels rely on newer CUDA primitives available in 515+. We'll mark features that are gated by driver versions in the matrix. For example Q4-optimizations for int8 require CUDA 11.8+ and certain cuBLAS versions
[08:55] Lina: License keys — we need a way to tie installs to a hardware fingerprint. Can license file include node IDs?

[09:10] Maya: We support hardware-locked licensing. The license file can include a whitelist of host identifiers (MAC, TPM, or a hardware UUID). We'll deliver an activation tool that computes a host fingerprint you paste into your portal to generate the license. For air-gapped, this is an offline text exchange and we can support bulk provisioning
[09:35] Priya: Audit logs — do you produce install and runtime audit logs for compliance?

[09:45] Carlos: Yes runtime logs include model loads, license checks, and auth events. Logs can be configured to ship to your SIEM via syslog/rsyslog. For air-gapped installs we provide a local log rotation policy and rolling retention
[10:00] Mark: KB about runtime: is it containerized as a sidecar or standalone service?

[10:10] Carlos: It's provided as a container runtime but we also provide a systemd-wrapped binary option for environments that prefer not to run container runtimes. The bundle includes both: OCI images for docker/crio and an extracted binary with required libs

[10:30] Maya: Quick note on packaging size for transport — we can split the bundle into chunked tarballs and provide a checksummed manifest so you can transfer via USB or internal artifact repo without corruption
[10:45] Samir: Good. For the pilot we want to measure warm-up time from a cold VM to first token — can you help instrument that?

[10:55] Carlos: We'll include a micro-benchmark that simulates traffic patterns and outputs time-to-first-token and steady-state throughput. We'll also provide scripts to toggle KV cache persistence on/off so you can measure warm vs cold starts

[11:15] Maya: On model licensing: if you want us to bring a specific open model variant, we can include that model in the bundle. For proprietary models we have a different packaging path — but for this pilot I assume open model family is fine
[11:35] Lina: We'll start with an open LLM, evaluate quantized Q4 vs fp16, then decide on model pinning
[11:50] Mark: How about metrics export when air-gapped; we can't push to your hosted dashboard. Do you support offline CSV exports?

[12:05] Carlos: Yes all telemetry can be written locally to files and rotated; we provide exporters to CSV/JSON that your SecOps can review. If you want encrypted bundles of metrics for periodic upload we can sign and encrypt with your public key
[12:25] Priya: Anything special about firewall rules? We're locked to allow only specific internal subnets

[12:35] Carlos: For on-prem Private control plane we need only occasional egress for license verification if you choose phone-home; for full air-gap we remove that requirement. Otherwise runtime talks only to local services — we provide a list of required ports for internal routing between nodes (gRPC ports, healthcheck) and we can run entirely on internal VLAN

[12:55] Maya: Recap: Redwood will provide offline bundle, signed manifest, driver matrix, runbook, and benchmarking scripts. Acme to provide GPU inventory, kernel details, and security constraints. Next step is delivery of the bundle and schedule pilot
[13:10] Lina: Sounds good. Two quick clarifying qs: 1) How are critical security patches handled if we can't internet-pull? 2) How long does support cover the air-gapped install?

[13:25] Maya: 1) For critical patches we produce a security patch bundle you can apply during maintenance windows; 2) Support SLAs for Private/On-prem are covered per our enterprise contract — we'll include support terms in the bundle. For pilots we offer dedicated SE time during the install week
[13:45] Mark: One odd thing — our infra team prefers using a single node as a control node to verify kernel modules before rolling; is that supported?
[13:55] Carlos: Yes the runbook includes a canary node procedure with smoke tests (GPU enumerations, sample inference, KV restore), plus automated rollback instructions
[14:15] Samir: We might want the runtime to run without containerd, can we do that?

[14:25] Carlos: Yes as mentioned earlier we provide a non-container binary. It includes a minimal bundling of the runtime and a recommended linker and lib set. We'll note supported distros and glibc bounds
[14:45] Priya: One more on cryptography: are the binaries reproducible? We need reproducible builds for full trust

[14:55] Maya: We have reproducible build docs for the runtime and a signed provenance file. For customers that require full reproducibility we can provide the build scripts and verify hashes on your side
[15:10] Mark: Ok great, last thing - how long would the pilot install typically take?

[15:20] Carlos: Most pilots complete initial install and basic benchmarking in 4-8 hours on a small testbed (2 nodes). Full validation and tuning across your cluster could take 1-2 weeks depending on tests
[15:40] Lina: Perfect, we'll aim for week of 2025-02-24 for the pilot window. We'll upload GPU inventory by 2025-02-19
[56:30] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the bundle and runbook; action items in the notes. Bye
[56:45] (call ended)
